blocks.text: Jeffrey Perez has come on as a Design Technician in the engineering group. He will draft the utility and stormwater sheets, and he is the hand the engineers will turn to when a set has to move quickly.

Jeffrey reports to Linda George, Project Engineer, who will set his assignments and his priorities. Much of his early work will be redlines, the marked-up sets an engineer needs turned on short notice. He works steadily and does not rush a callout; he checks it against the design memorandum rather than trusting memory, which is the discipline this office wants on the utility sheets. When a set goes out under his hand, he prepares the transmittal that accompanies it and notes what was sent, so the office has a record of every issue.

The first-period matters are straightforward. His station is on the CAD network, timekeeping is by project number on the weekly sheet, and the design memoranda for the active jobs are filed with their drawings where he can pull them. Every set still crosses Mark Todd's desk for review before the cover sheet is sealed, and Jeffrey has drafted to that kind of standard before, so we expect little breaking-in. The stormwater sheets in particular carry a great many small numbers, pipe sizes, inverts, and rim elevations, and a transposed figure there is the kind that reaches the field; he is to check those against the calculations and not against the last set. When a redline is unclear, he is to ask the engineer who marked it rather than guess at the intent.

The office is quiet through the end of the year, which is a fair time to learn the firm's way before the winter design work picks up. To start, Linda George will hand him the current stormwater redlines, and he can work those while he learns the firm's sheet standards.
